<!-- This vignette is precomputed because fitting the models needs
TensorFlow. Edit NonlinearBSS.Rmd.orig and run vignettes/precompile.R. -->



In nonlinear blind source separation the observed $p$-variate data $x$ are
assumed to be generated as $x = f(z)$, where $f$ is an unknown injective
function and $z$ are independent latent components. The aim is to recover $z$
from $x$. Without further assumptions this is impossible, but nonstationarity
of the components over time or space, or temporal dependence, makes them
identifiable.

This vignette illustrates three methods:

* `VAE()`: a variational autoencoder for i.i.d. data (a baseline; not
  identifiable),
* `iVAE()`: the identifiable variational autoencoder for any data with
  auxiliary variables,
* `iVAEar()`: iVAE with nonstationary autoregressive latent components.

All plots of the package are made with **ggplot2** and return
`ggplot` objects that can be modified further.

The models are fitted with TensorFlow through **keras3**. Install it once
with `keras3::install_keras()` and check the setup with `tf_available()`.

## Simulated data

`simulate_sources()` creates components whose means and variances change
over segments and `mix_data()` mixes them with a random neural network.


``` r
set.seed(1)
src <- simulate_sources(3, time = 1:3000, n_segments_time = 30)
x <- mix_data(src$sources, n_layers = 3)
```

## Auxiliary data

For iVAE the auxiliary variables $u$ should explain how the distribution of
the components changes. For a time series, indicators of time segments are a
simple choice:


``` r
A <- aux_matrix(aux_segments(100), x, time = 1:3000)
dim(A)
#> [1] 3000   30
```

Radial basis functions give a smooth and more flexible alternative:


``` r
A <- aux_matrix(aux_rbf(temporal_basis = c(9, 17, 37)), x, time = 1:3000)
dim(A)
#> [1] 3000   63
```

## Fitting iVAE


``` r
fit <- iVAE(x, aux_rbf(temporal_basis = c(9, 17, 37)), time = 1:3000, epochs = 50,
            verbose = 0, seed = 1)
fit
#> Identifiable variational autoencoder (iVAE)
#> 
#> Call: iVAE(x = x, aux = aux_rbf(temporal_basis = c(9, 17, 37)), time = 1:3000, 
#>     epochs = 50, seed = 1, verbose = 0)
#> Data: x (3000 observations, 3 variables, format matrix)
#> Latent components: 3
#> Auxiliary data: radial basis functions, spatial = 2, 9, temporal = 9, 17, 37 (gaussian) [63 variables]
#> Distributions: source gaussian, error gaussian (sigma 0.02)
#> ELBO: -3.1172
absolute_mean_correlation(fit$S, src$sources)
#> [1] 0.9565594
```

For comparison, the plain `VAE()` has no auxiliary variables. It is a
baseline whose components are not identifiable in general, so its recovery
is not guaranteed:


``` r
fit_vae <- VAE(x, latent_dim = 3, epochs = 50, verbose = 0, seed = 1)
absolute_mean_correlation(fit_vae$S, src$sources)
#> [1] 0.7132899
```

The mean correlation coefficient compares the estimates with the true
components up to permutation and sign; 1 means perfect recovery. The
components are stored as `fit$S` and are returned in the format of the data
by `components()`.


``` r
head(components(fit))
#>             IC1        IC2        IC3
#> [1,]  2.0283578  0.1393474 -0.4877269
#> [2,] -1.6412711 -0.6063424 -1.6819368
#> [3,]  1.0652925 -0.6113633 -1.2268908
#> [4,] -0.7140939  0.9349620 -0.6195569
#> [5,]  0.4349818 -1.6999949 -1.6443090
#> [6,] -0.8067482  0.4258073 -0.2712600
```

## Choosing the number of latent components

In practice the number of latent components is unknown. Following Sipilä
et al. (2025, *Neural Networks*; 2026, *Spatial Statistics*), it can be
selected by fitting models with different numbers of components $L$ and
maximising the profile AIC
$$\mathrm{pAIC} = \mathrm{ELBO} - L,$$
where the ELBO is the average evidence lower bound per observation. Here
the three sources are mixed into six observed variables, and models with one
to six components are compared:


``` r
x6 <- mix_data(src$sources, n_layers = 3, output_dim = 6)
sel <- select_latent_dim(x6, latent_dims = 1:6, aux = aux_segments(100),
                         time = 1:3000, epochs = 50, verbose = 0, seed = 1)
sel
#> Selection of the number of latent components
#> 
#>  latent_dim    elbo    pAIC selected
#>           1 -31.703 -32.703         
#>           2  -8.562 -10.562         
#>           3  -1.491  -4.491        *
#>           4  -1.696  -5.696         
#>           5  -1.585  -6.585         
#>           6  -1.631  -7.631         
#> 
#> Selected by the largest pAIC = ELBO - number of components: 3
```

The ELBO increases steeply until the true number of components and stays
nearly constant after that:


``` r
plot(sel)
```



![](figures/dimsel-1.png){width=100%}

The selected model is kept in the result. Models that were fitted
separately, for example in different sessions, can be compared with
`latent_dim_selection(list(fit1, fit2, ...))`. The models should differ only
in the number of components, since the ELBO also depends on the data, the
auxiliary variables and `error_dist_sigma`.

## Time series formats

Time series objects (`ts`, `xts`, `zoo`, `tsibble`) can be used directly, and
the results are returned in the same format.

The time points of these objects are measured in observation steps (here
months), as for matrices, so the auxiliary variables are specified in the same
way for all data formats:


``` r
xt <- ts(x, start = c(1800, 1), frequency = 12)
fit_ts <- iVAE(xt, aux_segments(100), epochs = 50, verbose = 0, seed = 1)
class(components(fit_ts))
#> [1] "mts"    "ts"     "matrix" "array"
absolute_mean_correlation(fit_ts$S, src$sources)
#> [1] 0.8748926
```


``` r
plot(fit_ts)
```



![](figures/ts-components-1.png){width=100%}

## A second simulated example: spatio-temporal data

`simulate_sources()` also creates spatio-temporal components, with
nonstationarity over space and time and, optionally, autoregressive
dependence. Here three latent components are observed at 60 random locations 
and at 40 time points, and the three components are mixed
into five observed variables with a two-layer random mixing function:


``` r
set.seed(1)
n_s <- 60
n_t <- 100
xy <- cbind(lon = runif(n_s), lat = runif(n_s))
coords <- xy[rep(seq_len(n_s), n_t), ]
time <- rep(seq_len(n_t), each = n_s)
src_st <- simulate_sources(3, coords = coords, time = time,
                           n_segments_space = 6, n_segments_time = 5,
                           ar_range = c(0.3, 0.9))
x_st <- mix_data(src_st$sources, n_layers = 2, output_dim = 5)
dat <- data.frame(x_st, coords, time = time)
vars_st <- colnames(x_st)
```

The data frame is used with the names of the coordinate, time and variable
columns. The radial basis functions of `aux_rbf()` are the auxiliary
variables. `VAE()` ignores the coordinates and times, `iVAE()` treats the
observations as independent given the auxiliary variables, and `iVAEar()` also
models the autoregressive dependence:


``` r
aux <- aux_rbf(spatial_basis = c(2, 9), temporal_basis = c(9, 17))
fit_st_vae <- VAE(dat[vars_st], latent_dim = 3, epochs = 60, verbose = 0, seed = 1)
fit_st_ivae <- iVAE(dat, aux, coords = c("lon", "lat"), time = "time",
                    vars = vars_st, latent_dim = 3, epochs = 60, verbose = 0,
                    seed = 1)
fit_st_ar <- iVAEar(dat, aux, coords = c("lon", "lat"), time = "time",
                    vars = vars_st, latent_dim = 3, epochs = 60, verbose = 0,
                    seed = 1)
sapply(list(VAE = fit_st_vae, iVAE = fit_st_ivae, iVAEar = fit_st_ar),
       function(f) absolute_mean_correlation(f$S, src_st$sources))
#>       VAE      iVAE    iVAEar 
#> 0.8760115 0.9822837 0.9917308
```

The estimated components as a map at the last time point, and as a time
series at the first location:


``` r
plot(fit_st_ar)
```



![](figures/st-map-1.png){width=100%}


``` r
plot(fit_st_ar, type = "series", series = 1)
```



![](figures/st-series-1.png){width=100%}

Since the result is a `ggplot` object, it can be customised with the usual
ggplot2 functions, for example `plot(fit_st_ar) + ggplot2::ggtitle("iVAEar")`.

## Spatio-temporal data

The data set `pollution_northern_italy` contains daily air quality
measurements at 50 stations. Here, the observations from January 2020 to April 2022 
are used for training,
May 2022 as forecasting test data. Five stations are set aside to test spatial
interpolation. The data frame is used with the column names of the
coordinates, time points and variables.


``` r
train_subset_time <- subset(pollution_northern_italy, time < as.Date("2022-05-01"))
stations <- unique(train_subset_time$AirQualityStation)
set.seed(2)
test_stations <- sample(stations, 5)
train_subset <- subset(train_subset_time, !AirQualityStation %in% test_stations)
vars <- c("mean_O3", "mean_NO2", "mean_PM10")
```

`iVAEar()` models the components as nonstationary autoregressive processes. 
The model is trained for 30 epochs with RBF auxiliary variables. 
The temporal RBFs are formed based on the seasonal time point (1 to 365)
instead of the absolute time point in order to allow the model to generalize better to future.


``` r
fit <- iVAEar(train_subset, aux = aux_rbf(spatial_basis = c(2, 9),
                                   temporal_basis = c(9, 17), seasonal_period = 365),
              coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), time = "time", vars = vars,
              epochs = 30, verbose = 0, seed = 1)
summary(fit)
#> Identifiable variational autoencoder with autoregressive components (iVAEar)
#> 
#> Call: iVAEar(x = train_subset, aux = aux_rbf(spatial_basis = c(2, 9), 
#>     temporal_basis = c(9, 17), seasonal_period = 365), coords = c("Longitude", 
#>     "Latitude"), time = "time", vars = vars, epochs = 30, seed = 1, 
#>     verbose = 0)
#> 
#> Data: train_subset 
#>   observations: 38295 
#>   variables: 3 
#>   format: data.frame 
#> Latent components: 3 
#> Autoregressive order: 1 
#> Auxiliary data: radial basis functions, spatial = 2, 9, temporal = 9, 17 (gaussian) + seasonal period 365 [114 variables]
#> 
#> Network: hidden units 128-128-128, auxiliary function 128-128-128, activation leaky_relu
#> Distributions: source gaussian, error gaussian
#> 
#> Training: 30 epochs, final loss 0.975
#> ELBO: -0.95145 
#> Largest absolute correlation between components: 0.463 
#> 
#> Prior variance of the standardised components over the data:
#>         0%    50%  100%
#> IC1 0.0118 0.0947 0.897
#> IC2 0.0339 0.1442 0.690
#> IC3 0.1039 0.3463 1.741
#> 
#> Autoregressive coefficients over the data:
#>  component lag     min  mean   max
#>        IC1   1 -0.1478 0.566 0.980
#>        IC2   1  0.1481 0.656 0.960
#>        IC3   1  0.0871 0.579 0.855
```


``` r
plot(fit, type = "history")
```



![](figures/history-1.png){width=100%}

The components can be shown as maps at a given day, or as time series at a
station:


``` r
plot(fit, time = as.Date("2022-04-01"))
```



![](figures/maps-1.png){width=100%}


``` r
plot(fit, type = "series", series = 1)
```



![](figures/series-1.png){width=100%}

## Forecasting and interpolation

The trend, variance and autoregressive coefficient functions can be
evaluated anywhere, and the components can be forecast from their last
values by iterating the autoregressive prior. With `space = "data"` the
predicted components are decoded to the observed variables. Here we
forecast the first week of May 2022, one to seven days after the end of the
training data:


``` r
test_time <- subset(pollution_northern_italy, 
                     time < as.Date("2022-05-08") & time > as.Date("2022-04-30"))
pred_time <- predict(fit, test_time, type = "forecast",
              coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), time = "time",
              space = "data")
head(pred_time)
#>       Longitude Latitude       time   mean_O3 mean_NO2 mean_PM10
#> 63663  11.43317 46.58967 2022-05-01 104.59662 4.334665  12.58798
#> 63664  11.43317 46.58967 2022-05-02  98.84446 4.166092  12.81774
#> 63665  11.43317 46.58967 2022-05-03  94.61120 4.104034  12.39065
#> 63666  11.43317 46.58967 2022-05-04  91.35274 4.034678  12.00895
#> 63667  11.43317 46.58967 2022-05-05  88.59262 3.947743  11.64543
#> 63668  11.43317 46.58967 2022-05-06  86.35072 3.904140  11.32179
```

The mean absolute error of the ozone forecasts by forecast day, compared
with the standard deviation of ozone in the test period:


``` r
round(c(MAE = mean(abs(pred_time$mean_O3 - test_time$mean_O3)),
        sd = sd(test_time$mean_O3)), 1)
#>  MAE   sd 
#> 13.5 18.8
```

Spatial interpolation uses the trend function at the locations of the five
stations not used in fitting:


``` r
test_space <- subset(train_subset_time, AirQualityStation %in% test_stations)
pred_space <- predict(fit, test_space, type = "trend",
                  coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), time = "time",
                  space = "data")
round(c(MAE = mean(abs(pred_space$mean_O3 - test_space$mean_O3)),
        sd = sd(test_space$mean_O3)), 1)
#>  MAE   sd 
#> 14.9 33.2
```

The predictions can be made also to future time points of new stations 
by using the trend function:

``` r
test_space_time <- subset(pollution_northern_italy, AirQualityStation %in% test_stations &
                          time < as.Date("2022-05-08") & time > as.Date("2022-04-30"))
pred_space_time <- predict(fit, test_space_time, type = "trend",
                  coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), time = "time",
                  space = "data")
round(c(MAE = mean(abs(pred_space_time$mean_O3 - test_space_time$mean_O3)),
        sd = sd(test_space_time$mean_O3)), 1)              
#>  MAE   sd 
#> 18.2 24.3
```

## Interpretation

`mshap()` measures how much each latent component contributes to each
observed variable by mean absolute kernel SHAP values of the decoder. The
scaled values sum to one for each variable. Sipilä et al. (2026, *Spatial
Statistics*) used them to interpret the latent components of weather and air
pollution data over Northern Italy.


``` r
ms <- mshap(fit, n_sample = 500, n_background = 50, seed = 1)
ms
#> Scaled mean absolute SHAP values (rows: variables, columns: components)
#> 
#>             IC1   IC2   IC3
#> mean_O3   0.364 0.584 0.053
#> mean_NO2  0.815 0.096 0.089
#> mean_PM10 0.375 0.111 0.514
#> Average   0.518 0.264 0.219
#> 
#> Based on 500 observations and 50 background observations.
```


``` r
plot(ms)
```



![](figures/mshap-1.png){width=100%}

## Spatial data formats

With an `sf` or `sftime` object the coordinates and time points are taken
from the object, and the results are again `sf` objects. For points, the
coordinates are those of the geometry:


``` r
s <- sf::st_as_sf(dat, coords = c("lon", "lat"))
fit_sf <- iVAEar(s, aux, time = "time", vars = vars_st, latent_dim = 3,
                 epochs = 60, verbose = 0, seed = 1)
head(components(fit_sf), 3)
#> Simple feature collection with 3 features and 4 fields
#> Geometry type: POINT
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: 0.2655087 ymin: 0.2936034 xmax: 0.5728534 ymax: 0.9128759
#> CRS:           NA
#>   time        IC1       IC2        IC3                    geometry
#> 1    1 -0.1744864 0.5799103 -1.0028925 POINT (0.2655087 0.9128759)
#> 2    1  1.0015271 0.3588701 -0.1335403 POINT (0.3721239 0.2936034)
#> 3    1  0.5771135 0.6203762 -1.1136303 POINT (0.5728534 0.4590657)
```

Spatio-temporal objects of the **sp** and **spacetime** packages (`STFDF`)
are also accepted, and the results are returned as `STFDF` objects:


``` r
sp_pts <- sp::SpatialPoints(xy)
st <- spacetime::STFDF(sp_pts, as.POSIXct("2020-01-01", tz = "UTC") + 86400 * (seq_len(n_t) - 1),
                       data.frame(x_st))
fit_stfdf <- iVAEar(st, aux, latent_dim = 3, epochs = 20, verbose = 0, seed = 1)
class(components(fit_stfdf))
```

## Large data

For large spatio-temporal data the auxiliary matrix can become very large.
With `batch_aux = TRUE` the auxiliary variables are computed for each batch
inside the network from the coordinates and time points, which gives the
same model with much less memory:


``` r
fit <- iVAEar(pollution_northern_italy, aux_rbf(),
              coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), time = "time", vars = vars,
              batch_aux = TRUE)
```

## Saving models

The trained weights are stored in the fitted object, so models can be saved
with `save_nlbss()` (or `saveRDS()`) and used in a new session:


``` r
file <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
save_nlbss(fit, file)
fit2 <- load_nlbss(file)
all.equal(predict(fit2, type = "trend"), predict(fit, type = "trend"))
#> [1] TRUE
```
